questions.q: A step says: "Keep checking the shoebox until Mr Okafor's receipt appears." Which property of an algorithm does it break?
questions.explain: If the receipt is not in the box, you check forever. An algorithm must always stop, so it needs a rule for the "not there" case: stop after the last receipt and report "not found".

questions.q: A step says: "Count the big sales." Which property does it break?
questions.explain: "Big" means different things to different people, so two people following the step get different counts. A precise version says "sales above ₦10,000", and even then you must decide whether exactly ₦10,000 counts.

questions.q: A method says: "Look through every receipt in the box, one by one." Nothing else. What is missing for it to be an algorithm?
questions.explain: It does work, and it stops, but it produces no result. An algorithm must give at least one output, such as the matching receipt or "not found".
options: An output: it never reports anything

questions.q: Which step breaks the effective property, that every step can actually be carried out?
questions.explain: Nobody, and no computer, can do that step with the information available. The other steps are simple actions on data you have.
options: Add the price to the total
If the stock is below 5, add the item to the reorder list
Find the medicine the customer will need next month
Move the smallest receipt to the sorted row

questions.q: Which three shapes of step are enough to build any algorithm?
questions.explain: Steps one after another (sequence), choosing a path (decision, if) and doing steps again (repetition, loops). Searching, counting and sorting are all built from these three.

questions.q: "If the customer has a prescription, charge no VAT; otherwise charge 7.5%." Which shape is this?
questions.explain: It chooses between two paths based on a condition. In JavaScript that is if and else.

questions.q: "For each shelf, from the first to the last, check how many items are left." Which shape is this?
questions.explain: The same step is done again for every shelf. In JavaScript that is a loop, such as for (const shelf of shelves).

questions.q: A list has 1,000 customer names in no particular order. Using linear search, how many names must you look at to be sure that "Nwosu" is not in it?
questions.explain: Any name you skip could be the one. To prove something is missing, linear search has to look at every item. That is why "not found" is the slowest case.

questions.q: You can find a word in a paper dictionary without reading from "A". Why?
questions.explain: Sorted data lets you rule out half of what is left with each look. That faster method, binary search, only works because the order is known.
options: The words are sorted, so you can open the middle and jump towards the word
You remember where every word is

questions.q: In the search loop, what does break do when the name matches?
questions.explain: break leaves the loop it is in. Once the receipt is found there is no reason to keep looking, and the position counter stays at the match.
options: It skips to the next name
It stops the loop straight away, so the remaining names are not looked at

questions.q: To find the best day's profit, why start "best so far" at the first item of the list rather than at 0?
questions.explain: With profits of -2000, -500 and -1200, nothing is bigger than 0, so 0 would be reported. Starting with a real item guarantees the answer is one of the actual values.
options: If every value is negative, starting at 0 reports ₦0, which is not in the list
0 is not allowed as a starting value in JavaScript
The first item is always the biggest

questions.q: Which algorithm usually gives you a list with fewer items than you started with?
questions.explain: Filtering keeps only the items that match a rule. Transformation and sorting keep every item; totalling gives a single number.

questions.q: You transform a list of 8 prices from naira to kobo. How many items does the new list have?
questions.explain: A transformation makes one new item from every item, so the result has the same length. Checking that the lengths match is a quick test for any transformation.
options: Fewer than 8, depending on the prices

questions.q: "Make a list of all invoices that have not been paid." Which algorithm is this?
questions.explain: It keeps the items that match a rule (unpaid) and produces a new, shorter list. Searching would find just one; counting would give a number.

questions.q: "Add 7.5% VAT to every price on the board." Which algorithm is this?
questions.explain: Every item becomes a new item by the same rule. The board has as many prices afterwards as before.

questions.q: "How many students scored above 70?" Which algorithm answers this?
questions.explain: Start at 0 and add 1 for every score that matches the rule. The output is a single number.

questions.q: Selection sort on the pile 9, 4, 7, 1: each round moves the smallest item from the pile to the end of the sorted row. What is the sorted row after two rounds?
questions.explain: Round 1 finds 1, the smallest of 9, 4, 7, 1. Round 2 finds 4, the smallest of what is left (9, 4, 7). The row is 1, 4, and the pile is 9, 7.

questions.q: Why does [4500, 12000].sort() put 12000 first?
questions.explain: Without instructions, sort compares text. For numbers, pass (a, b) => a - b. The general lesson: never trust a sort until you have checked it on an input whose right order you know.
options: Because the default sort compares items as text, and "1" comes before "4"
Because sort always reverses the list
Because of a bug in JavaScript that was never fixed

questions.q: A day has no sales. The average algorithm divides the total by the number of sales. What should the program do?
questions.explain: 0 divided by 0 is NaN ("not a number"). An empty list is a normal input, so the algorithm needs a proper output for it. Dividing by 1 would report an average of ₦0, which is also wrong.
options: Print NaN, because that is the correct answer
Crash, because an empty list is an error
Check for an empty list first and report something sensible, such as "No sales today"

questions.q: Which set of test inputs is best for a search algorithm?
questions.explain: Bugs hide at the edges: loops that stop one step early miss the last item, bad starting values break the first, and the "not found" path is the one people forget.
options: Three names from the middle of a long list
An empty list, the first name, the last name, and a name that is not there
Only names that are definitely in the list

questions.q: The list has two receipts for "Okafor", at positions 2 and 4. The search uses break when it finds a match. Which does it report?
questions.explain: The search stops at the first match. Whether "the first one" is what Mrs Adeyemi needs (perhaps she wants the latest) is a question to ask; duplicates belong in your test list.

questions.q: In a test that searches for several names, one after another, why must position and found be set back to their starting values at the start of each search?
questions.explain: If found is still true from the first search, a later missing name looks "found". Every accumulator must start fresh for each run of the algorithm.
options: Because JavaScript deletes variables after a loop
Otherwise the second search starts with the first search's leftover values
It does not matter where they are set

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 7.5% of 8,000 is 8,000 × 7.5 ÷ 100 = 600. The steps run in sequence, each using the result of the one before.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The counter goes up before each comparison: 1 for Eze, 2 for Musa, 3 for Bello. At Bello, break stops the loop, so Okafor is never counted.

questions.q: This search forgot break. What does it print?
questions.explain: found is set correctly, but the loop keeps going, so position keeps counting to the end of the list. Without break, the position reported is the length of the list, not where Musa is.

questions.q: The supplier's bonus is for sales above ₦10,000. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only 10,001 and 25,000 are above 10,000. Exactly 10,000 is not above it. The boundary value is in the list on purpose.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The total is 10,000 and there are 3 sales, so the average is 10,000 ÷ 3. Computers store decimals with limited precision, so the last digit comes out as 5. Money needs proper rounding, which a later lesson covers.

questions.q: Every day was a loss. What does this print?
questions.explain: No profit is greater than 0, so best never changes and the starting value is reported. It is not even in the list. Starting with profits[0] would give -300.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Positions 0 and 2 have 4 and 5 in stock, both "5 or fewer". The filter pushes the name at the same position, not the stock number.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each amount is multiplied by 100 and added to the new list. A transformation keeps the length: 3 in, 3 out.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The default sort compares text: "100" starts with "1", which comes before "2", which comes before "3". To sort numbers, use amounts.sort((a, b) => a - b).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: List positions start at 0, so sales[0] is 4500 and sales[1] is the second item, 800. length counts the items: 3.

questions.q: No orders arrived today. What does this print?
questions.explain: With an empty list the loop body runs zero times, so the counter keeps its starting value, 0. That is the right answer, and it is why counts start at 0.
options: Nothing: the loop crashes on an empty list

questions.q: Two suppliers quote the same lowest price. What does this print?
questions.explain: Juhel's 17,000 is not less than the 17,000 already found, so the best so far stays Fidson. With <= it would be Juhel. Ties are a test case worth deciding on purpose.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: i starts at 0 and the loop runs while i < 3, so it takes 0, 1 and 2: exactly the positions in the list. With i <= items.length it would run once too often and print 3 undefined.

questions.q: Count the orders whose status is "pending" and print Pending: 2.
questions.explain: Counting: start at 0, go through every item, add 1 when the item matches the rule.

questions.q: Add up the day's sales and print Takings: ₦21300.
questions.explain: Totalling is counting's twin: instead of adding 1 for each item, add the item itself.

questions.q: Find the biggest sale with the "best so far" algorithm, starting from the first sale, and print Biggest: 9800.
questions.explain: Remember the biggest seen so far and replace it whenever a bigger one comes along. Starting with sales[0] means the answer is always a real sale.

questions.q: Every day this week was a loss, so this prints Best: 0, which is not one of the days. Fix the starting value so it prints Best: -300.
questions.explain: Starting at 0 assumes the answer is at least 0. Starting with the first real value makes no assumption, so it works for any list that has at least one item.

questions.q: Search the list for "Musa" and print his position counting from 1: Musa is number 4. Stop looking once you find him.
questions.explain: Count each name as you look at it and stop with break at the match. Without break the counter would run on to 5. A complete search also needs a found flag for the "not found" case.

questions.q: Make a new list with only the scores of 50 or more, and print it: [ 72, 50, 91 ].
questions.explain: Filtering keeps the items that match the rule, in their original order, and leaves the original list unchanged. 50 is on the boundary and passes because the rule says "or more".

questions.q: Transform the naira prices into kobo (multiply by 100) in a new list, and print it: [ 50000, 120000, 1500 ].
questions.explain: A transformation makes one new item from every item by the same rule, so three prices in give three prices out.

questions.q: With no sales this prints Average: NaN. Add a check so that when the list is empty it prints No sales today instead, and otherwise prints the average as before.
questions.explain: An empty list is a normal input. Checking sales.length === 0 before dividing gives it a sensible output instead of NaN.
